latin.305:
§. II.
Posterior Controversiarum Classis Autores ac disputatores habet, quà res maximè controversas, Joh. Brentii, ubiquitatis seu omnipraesentiae Corporis Christi; Jac. Andreae, oralis hujus Corporis manducationis superadditae, & Aegidii Hunnii, Praedestinationis ex praevisa Fide, praecipuorum ac famosissimorum Doctorum; quà modum autem controvertendi acerbiorem, Flacii Illyrici, inquietissimi hominis Ingenii, Discipulos: Verbô unô, eos, qui si non omnes, certè quàm plurimi, in verba Formulae Concordiae, etiam damnatoria, non minus, re ipsâ, quàm in verba ipsius Scripturae S. sibi jurandum ducunt.
latin.306: Numerum habet, quà principales Controversias, Ternarium, seu tres potiùs dogmatum Christianorum articulos concernentem: De S. Coenâ primum; alterum, ex hoc enatum, de Persona Christi, tandemque adjectum tertium de Praedestinatione; Quà minus Principales, innumerum, & pro intempestivo zelo, quandoque etiam pro nuda Autorum libidine, indies augendum.
latin.307: Ut inde Autori nostro haec controversiarum Classis, in triplici differentia jure collocetur, quarum aliae nude confictae sint, quaestiones facti, non juris, quales Reformatorum nemini unquam in mentem venerunt, e. gr. Num Deus sit Autor Peccati? in Capite de Providentia Dei; Num omnipotens? in Capite de Praesentia Corporali in Coena; Num misericors? in doctrina de gratia, &c. Aliae minoris momenti, de ritibus & ceremoniis adiaphoris, in quibus facile Reformatos haberent obsequentes Lutherani: Aliae denique reales magis, ad tria dicta Capita Principalia pertinentes. Conf. in Annot. preced. cit. Tractatulum nost. Germanicum, Kurzer Entwurff der Einigkeit der Evangelisch-Lutherischen und Reformirten §.XIII. & seqq.
latin.308: Modum tractandi plerumque acerbiorem, omnibusque tàm piis Christianis quibuscunque, quàm ipsis Theologis cordatioribus exosum, ac res sacras, & Sacrum ordinem, & Causam Protestanticam, turpiter prostituentem, & tantum non pessimum in modum infamantem, etiam vel infra vulgi ipsarumque vetularum rixas, altercationes, calumnias, verba contumeliosa atque propudia projectum,
latin.309: praeterea cum Damnationibus opinionum adversantium, utut maximè innocuarum, verarum, seu falsarum, certè non fundamentalium, conjunctum promiscuè: quales damnationes in Epitome articulorum, de quibus Controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos August. Confessionis, quam plurimae leguntur, tàm in opiniones Fratrum Luthericorum, ab eodem Lutheri nomine appellatorum, nonnullas, quam in Reformatorum plures latas, e. g. in has,
latin.310: Fidem non justificare sine bonis operibus, i. e. Fidem solitariam non justificare, Antithes. XI. ad Artic. 3. p. m. 560. Bona opera necessaria ad salutem esse, Antit. I. ad Art. 4. p. m. 563. Fidem in Christum non amitti, & Spiritum S. nihilominus in homine habitare, etiamsi sciens volens (puta actu duntaxat, non habitu, & semiplenâ voluntate) peccet homo. Ibidem, Ant. 3. Corpus Christi in S. Coena non corporaliter una cum pane sumi, sed tantum Panem & Vinum ore accipi, Corpus verò Christi spiritualiter, i. e. Fide sumi. Antit. 5. ad Art. 7. p. m. 574. Fideles Corpus & sanguinem Christi non in Pane & Vino Coenae Dominicae quaerere, sed oculos in Coelum attollere, & inde Corpus Christi petere debere. Ibid. Antith. 15. p. 575. Infideles & impaenitentes Christianos in Coena Domini, non verum Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, sed Panem tantum & vinum sumere. Antit. 16. p. m. 575. Christum secundum Humanitatem (eóque finitam Naturam) Omnipotentiae, aliarumque Proprietatum Divinae Naturae (eóque Infinitarum), prorsus non esse capacem. Christo, item, secundum humanitatem, datam quidem maximam potestatem in Coelo & in Terra, videlicet majorem & ampliorem, quàm omnes Angeli & Creaturae acceperunt, sed tamen cum Omnipotentia Dei nullam habere communicationem, neg. Omnipotentiam divinam illi (h. e. humanae Naturae) datam esse, Antit. 15. & 16. ad Art. 8. p. m. 582.

pass_a.305: §. II. The Posterior Class of Controversies has as Authors and disputators, as to the matters most contested, the chief and most famous Doctors John Brenz (of the ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ’s Body), Jacob Andreae (of the oral manducation of this Body superadded), and Aegidius Hunnius (of Predestination from foreseen Faith); but as to the more acerbic mode of controverting, the Disciples of Flacius Illyricus, a man of most restless Ingenuity: in a word, those who — if not all, certainly the great majority — lead themselves to swear by the words of the Formula of Concord, even the damnatory ones, no less, in the very matter, than by the words of Holy Scripture itself.
pass_a.306: It has a Number, as to the principal Controversies, a Ternary — or rather concerning three articles of Christian dogmas: first On the Sacred Supper; second, sprung from this, On the Person of Christ; and third finally added On Predestination; but as to the less Principal, an innumerable number, and one to be increased day by day by intemperate zeal, and sometimes even by the bare libido of the Authors.
pass_a.307: So that for our Author this Class of controversies is rightly placed in a triple difference, of which some are nude fabrications — questions of fact, not of right — such as never entered any Reformer’s mind, e.g. Whether God is the Author of Sin? in the Chapter on God’s Providence; Whether omnipotent? in the Chapter on Corporeal Presence in the Supper; Whether merciful? in the doctrine of grace, etc. Others of lesser moment, on adiaphorous rites and ceremonies, in which Lutherans would easily have the Reformed obedient: Others finally more real, pertaining to the three said Principal Heads. Compare in the preceding Annotation the cited German tract of ours, Short Sketch of the Unity of the Evangelical-Lutheran and Reformed §.XIII and following.
pass_a.308: The Mode of treating is for the most part more acerbic, hated by all pious Christians whatever no less than by the more cordate Theologians themselves, and foully prostituting sacred things and the Sacred order and the Protestant Cause, and all but infaming them in the worst way — projected even below the quarrels, altercations, calumnies, contumelious words and shamelessnesses of the vulgar and of old women themselves —
pass_a.309: further, joined promiscuously with Damnations of opposing opinions, however most innocuous, true or false, certainly not fundamental: such damnations as are read in great number in the Epitome of the articles concerning which Controversies have arisen among the Theologians of the Augsburg Confession — laid both against some opinions of the Lutheric Brethren called by the same name of Luther, and against more of the Reformeds — for example against these:
pass_a.310: That Faith does not justify without good works, i.e. that solitary Faith does not justify (Antithesis XI to Art. 3, p. m. 560); That good works are necessary to salvation (Antit. I to Art. 4, p. m. 563); That Faith in Christ is not lost, and the Holy Spirit nevertheless dwells in a man, even if he sins knowingly and willingly (that is, in act only, not in habit, and with half-full will) (Ibid., Ant. 3); That Christ’s Body in the Sacred Supper is not taken corporeally together with the bread, but only Bread and Wine are received by mouth, while Christ’s Body is taken spiritually, i.e. by Faith (Antit. 5 to Art. 7, p. m. 574); That the faithful ought not to seek Christ’s Body and blood in the Bread and Wine of the Lord’s Supper, but to lift eyes to Heaven and thence ask Christ’s Body (Ibid. Antith. 15, p. 575); That unbelieving and impenitent Christians in the Lord’s Supper take not the true Body and Blood of Christ but only Bread and wine (Antit. 16, p. m. 575); That Christ according to the Humanity (and so a finite Nature) is altogether incapable of Omnipotence and the other Properties of the Divine Nature (and so of Infinite ones); likewise that to Christ according to the humanity there is indeed given the greatest power in Heaven and on Earth — greater and ampler than all Angels and Creatures received — yet that He has no communication with God’s Omnipotence, nor is divine Omnipotence given to it (i.e. to the human Nature) (Antit. 15 & 16 to Art. 8, p. m. 582).

305: §. II. The posterior class has, for the hottest points, Brenz on the ubiquity or omnipresence of Christ’s body, Andreae on oral manducation of that body added on top, and Hunnius on predestination from foreseen faith.
For the harsher style of fight it has Flacius Illyricus’s disciples — a most restless ingenuity.
In a word: those who (if not all, then most) bind themselves to the Formula of Concord’s words — even the damnatory ones — as tightly as to Holy Scripture itself.
306: As to principal controversies the number is a ternary: first the Sacred Supper; then, sprung from it, the Person of Christ; and third, Predestination.
The lesser ones are countless, and they grow daily by intemperate zeal — sometimes by bare authorial whim.
307: Our author therefore sorts this class into a threefold difference.

Some items are bare fabrications — questions of fact, not of right — that never entered any Reformer’s mind (Is God the author of sin? Is He omnipotent in bodily supper-presence? Is He merciful in the doctrine of grace?).
Others are lesser adiaphorous rites, where Lutherans would easily find the Reformed compliant.
Others again are more real and touch the three principal heads (see our German Short Sketch of Unity, §.XIII ff.).
308: The mode of treatment is usually more acerbic.
Pious Christians and the more sober theologians alike hate it.

It foully prostitutes sacred things, the sacred order, and the Protestant cause — and nearly brands them with the worst infamy — sunk even below the quarrels, calumnies, and shameless abuse of the crowd and of old women.
309: It is also promiscuously joined to damnations of opposing opinions — however harmless, whether true or false, and certainly not fundamental.

In the Epitome of articles on controversies among Augsburg Confession theologians, such damnations abound — against some opinions of Luther’s own-named brethren, and against more on the Reformed side — for example these:
310: That faith does not justify without good works (i.e. solitary faith does not justify); that good works are necessary to salvation; that faith in Christ is not lost and the Spirit still dwells even when someone sins knowingly in act only.

That Christ’s body is not taken corporeally with the bread but only bread and wine by mouth, the body spiritually by faith; that the faithful must look to heaven rather than seek the body in the supper elements; that unbelieving communicants receive only bread and wine.

That Christ according to the humanity is incapable of divine omnipotence and the other infinite properties; that the greatest power given to His humanity still has no communication with God’s omnipotence (Epitome antitheses to Arts. 3–4, 7–8).
Stop before §. III (if Lutherans dropped this acerbic mode / swapped damnations for bare rejections, the door to fraternity would stand open).
